newsitem.title: UK: UK may buy power plant to burn mad cow remains.
newsitem.headline: UK may buy power plant to burn mad cow remains.

text.p: The British government is considering buying an old power station to burn the remains of almost 1-1/2 million cattle slaughtered in the fight to eradicate mad cow disease, Agriculture Minister Jack Cunningham said on Tuesday.
He said ministers had been forced to consider this option because the owners of currently operating power plants had quoted "unreasonable" prices to the government for carrying out the work.

Since the mad cow crisis erupted in March 1996, 1.42 million British cattle have been slaughtered and sent for rendering into manageable by-products, leaving huge mountains of meat, bonemeal and tallow in store.
The slaughtering programme is meant to allay European Union fears about mad cow disease. If humans eat infected beef, they risk death from a brain-wasting malady, Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD).
The EU has banned exports of British beef until it is satisfied with the measures London is taking.
Cunningham told BBC radio in an interview that the government had been advised that incineration or landfill were both possible ways of clearing out the slaughtered cattle stores.
But he said "what we regard as unreasonable costs are being suggested by other people to incinerate this material".
Therefore the government was considering "the purchase of a mothballed or redundant power station and the retro-fitting of it to make it suitable for the burning of this material," Cunningham said.
"That is a possibility, that is being examined. It is no further forward than that," he added.
Cunningham has said the government faces a possible four billion pound ($6.66 billion) bill for tackling mad cow disease, known formally as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy.
Justifying recently announced cuts in compensation for farmers forced to slaughter cattle, he said the government "just can't go on with expenditure for which no provision has been made."
However, the beef industry saw its first chink of light in a gloomy situation last week when burger chain McDonald's announced it was ending a ban of home-grown beef in its 764 British restaurants.
